lesson.text: Quick memory: what did the Egyptians write on? (Papyrus, made from reeds.) Now travel east to the Indus River, in today's Pakistan and north-west India. People there built some of the best-planned cities of the ancient world.

The Indus Valley civilisation was at its biggest from about 2600 to 1900 BC. Archaeologists have found over 1,000 towns and villages. The biggest cities were Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, which was built about 2500 BC.

Mohenjo-daro was planned before it was built. Its main streets were straight, running north to south and east to west in a grid. Houses were built of baked bricks, and the bricks were the same shape all over the land.

Most houses had a bathroom, and many had a toilet. Dirty water flowed into covered brick drains along the streets, with holes where workers could clean them out. Few cities in the ancient world had anything as good.

The Great Bath is a pool about 12 m long and 7 m wide. Fitted bricks and a layer of tar made it watertight. Nobody knows exactly what it was for; perhaps people washed there before special ceremonies.

Traders stamped their goods with small square stone seals carved with animals, like bulls and elephants, and a line of signs. Indus seals have been found in Mesopotamia, so the two lands traded. But nobody can read the signs!
Other mysteries: no great palace or royal tomb has been found, so we do not know who ruled. Around 1900 BC the cities slowly emptied, perhaps because rivers changed course and the rains grew weaker.

Try it in the world: plan a city on a grid with straight streets and same-sized brick houses. Put a covered drain under every street, then add a great bath. Next: bronze and oracle bones in Shang China.

exercises.prompt: Which river gave the Indus Valley civilisation its name?
exercises.hint: The answer is in the name!
exercises.explain: The Indus River flows through today's Pakistan; the civilisation grew along it and its branches.

exercises.prompt: What ran under the streets of Mohenjo-daro?
exercises.hint: Where did the water from the bathrooms go?
exercises.explain: Covered brick drains carried dirty water away from the houses.

exercises.prompt: The streets of Mohenjo-daro were planned in straight lines.
exercises.hint: Picture the city from above: like a grid.
exercises.explain: True: the main streets ran north to south and east to west, making blocks like a grid.

exercises.prompt: Which country is most of the Indus Valley in today?
exercises.hint: The Indus River flows through it to the sea.
exercises.explain: Pakistan, with some of the cities in north-west India.

exercises.prompt: What were the small stone seals used for?
exercises.hint: Traders needed to mark whose goods were whose.
exercises.explain: Seals were pressed into clay on goods to show who they belonged to, a bit like a label.

exercises.prompt: We can read the Indus script today.
exercises.hint: Remember: one of history's great mysteries.
exercises.explain: False: nobody has worked out the Indus signs yet, so we cannot read what they say.

exercises.prompt: How do we know the Indus people traded with Mesopotamia?
exercises.hint: What would a trader carry far away?
choices: Indus seals were found in Mesopotamia
a king wrote a book about it last year
they used the same money as us
exercises.explain: Indus seals and beads have been found in Mesopotamia, so goods travelled between the two lands.

exercises.prompt: Why was it helpful that bricks were the same shape everywhere?
exercises.hint: Think of building with blocks that all fit together.
choices: builders could plan and build walls well
exercises.explain: Same-shaped bricks fit together neatly, so builders anywhere could plan and build strong, straight walls.

exercises.prompt: Match each Indus find to what it tells us.
exercises.hint: Ask each find: what was it used for?
exercises.explain: Drains kept streets clean; the Great Bath may have been for special washing; seals marked traded goods; toy carts show that children played.

exercises.prompt: Put these in order, earliest first.
exercises.hint: BC years count down to AD 1. The 1920s are AD.
items: the Great Pyramid is finished (about 2560 BC)
exercises.explain: 2560 BC, then 2500 BC, then 1900 BC, then the 1920s, when archaeologists began to dig.

exercises.prompt: No palaces or royal tombs have been found in the Indus cities. What can we say?
exercises.hint: Good detectives only say what the evidence shows.
choices: we do not know who ruled them
they definitely had a great king
exercises.explain: The planned cities show that someone organised them, but without palaces, tombs or readable writing we do not know who ruled.

exercises.prompt: Why do archaeologists think the Indus cities emptied?
exercises.hint: Farmers need water. What if the water changed?
choices: perhaps rivers moved and the rains grew weaker
a volcano buried them all in one day
exercises.explain: Many think rivers moved and the rains weakened, so farming got harder and people slowly moved away. It is still being studied.

exercises.prompt: Few cities in the ancient world had drains as good as Mohenjo-daro's.
exercises.hint: Remember how dirty water left the houses.
exercises.explain: True: covered brick drains with holes for cleaning were far ahead of their time.

exercises.prompt: The Great Bath is about 12 m long and 7 m wide. How far is it all the way round its edge, in metres?
exercises.hint: Add all four sides: two long sides and two short sides.

exercises.prompt: The Indus civilisation was at its biggest from about 2600 BC to 1900 BC. For about how many years was that?
exercises.hint: BC years count down: take the smaller number from the bigger one.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: what archaeologists know, or what is still a mystery?
items: the streets were in a grid
what the Great Bath was for
exercises.hint: Could you see it in the ruins, or does it need writing we cannot read?
exercises.explain: We know: the grid of streets, the covered drains and the trade with Mesopotamia, from what was dug up. Mysteries: the signs cannot be read, so we do not know who ruled or what the Great Bath was for.
